newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Japanese, German banks likely to set up in NZ.
newsitem.headline: Japanese, German banks likely to set up in NZ.

text.p: New Zealand is set to welcome two major new entrants to its banking scene in the form of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi and Deutsche Bank AG, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Deutsche is Germany's biggest bank, while Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi is the largest in the world.
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Deputy Governor Dick Lang confirmed the bank had received two applications for bank registration although he declined to identify the banks.
Bank of Tokyo and Deutsche Bank would neither confirm nor deny they had made applications, although one of the banks said it expects to make an announcement later this month.
"The fact that people are looking to set up banks here is positive from a New Zealand perspective," Lang told Reuters.
"From a New Zealand perspective there are clear advantages of having a spread of banks. We have a fair amount of Australian involvement, obviously a broader range of banks is desirable," Lang said.
Massey University Banking Professor Chris Moore said such a move by two of the world's heavyweight banks was significant.
"These are big players," he said, adding he would expect their New Zealand operations to mirror those in Australia, where they are largely wholesale and specialist operations.

Godfrey Boyce, banking partner at accounting firm KPMG, said the impending moves reflected the globalisation of the industry. "There aren't huge new opportunities in New Zealand, it's more a reflection of the banks' need to serve customers anywhere in the world," he said.
New Zealand has some 16 registered banks but none from Japan and only two from continental Europe.

Japanese banks have shunned New Zealand mainly because of the 1989 collapse of merchant bank DFC New Zealand Ltd. DFC collapsed dramatically with debts of over NZ$2.2 billion, mostly to large and influential Japanese banks, but virtually all money owed was recovered and repaid.
Lang did not see the absence of banks from Japan in New Zealand as an important gap, despite rapidly growing trade.

"I'm not sure to what extent there has been a gap. For example the Bank of Tokyo have had a representative office here for some time. Lots of Japanese bankers visit New Zealand regularly. So setting up an operation here for any bank is really just another step further along the track."
Deutsche has since the late 1980s had a presence through its wholly-owned Australasian investment banking arm, Bain & Co.

Some banking industry commentators have noted that the Lloyds-TSB -owned National Bank of New Zealand could be up for sale, having lost to Westpac Banking Corp in its bid to take over Trust Bank New Zealand.
However, industry analysts doubted Bank of Tokyo or Deutsche would be likely buyers of National, being large, non-English banks centred in different hemispheres.
They are more likely to be taking advantage of New Zealand's time window as the first foreign exchange market in the world to open each day, and opportunities to conduct trade finance.
Only two continental European banks operate in New Zealand -- Compagnie Financiere de Suez of France and Dutch rural bank specialist Rabobank Nederland, which opened its doors last year.

However, Moore noted that the banking scene in New Zealand was intensely competitive and several big name banks had relinquished their banking registration after finding the going too tough. He expects the competition to heat up further.
